title: the WSG portable shelter mechanics and rest and comfort slice with Table 37 - the shelter kits and the Table 36 column semantics, the sleep requirements and the five-band lack-of-sleep effects, printed pp. 63-64
audit_label: R473 WSG sleep and shelter pin audit
audit_comment: The Table 37 grid (the five average-rest bands by eight effect columns: the Dexterity, Strength, Wisdom and Constitution check ladders, the to-hit penalties, the Climbing and Movement reductions, the Weight Allowance multiples), the shelter kit descriptions, the occupancy rulings, the setup and takedown discipline, the moisture and wind resistance semantics, the life span point economy with the category degradation, the 16-hour active day with the 5-hour sleep requirement, the two-day trigger with the one-night negation and the movement rate semantics - every const, bool and table cell verified against the model.

banner.title: R473: the WSG PORTABLE SHELTER MECHANICS and REST AND COMFORT slice with TABLE 37 - the shelter kits (the poor covering loosely stitched of several pieces with wind through the seams and no anchoring gear or rope provided, what an unskilled maker ends up with; the adequate kit of at least two poles - a backbone ridgepole and a cross-brace - with tighter stitching and stakes driven through the covering edges; the good kit of at least four poles with the covering pieces stitched tightly and overlapped like shingles so no seams are exposed and reinforced edge holes for damage-free anchoring; the superior kit of at least six poles making a strong frame, a tailored covering of as few pieces as possible with reinforced seams - a true structure, the next best thing to a miner's shack), the occupancy (a small shelter one human-sized or two smaller characters plus all their gear, twice as many in close quarters; a medium two human-sized, twice as many close; a large four by design, five or six sleeping with gear stored outside, seven or eight in close quarters and no more than eight), the setup and takedown discipline (a second character reducing setup by 1 turn; a rope use proficient character halving the setup time rounded up with or without help; the 1/2/3-turn setup minimums by size; the takedown in 1 turn less than setup regardless of helpers, halved by rope use proficiency, with the 5-round/1-turn/2-turn minimums; the poor and adequate kits assuming the characters bring their own rope), the moisture rule (precip heavier than the value gets through as a storm one step lighter; a superior shelter protecting from even a downpour unless the wind is too strong or the storm separates it from its moorings), the wind rules (the greatest velocity withstood without leaking; every 10 mph above the number a 5 mph wind felt inside; above twice the number a 25% chance per 10 mph each hour of wind damage leaving the shelter useless until repaired; the book example of the 20-mph poor shelter feeling 5/10/15/20 mph at 30/40/50/60 with 25% then 50% damage per hour), the life span (the shelter's hit points: 1 point per three times put up, 1 per non-damaging over-wind exposure, 2 per equal-intensity precip, 4 per greater; a superior, good or adequate shelter dropping to the next category's maximum treated as that category; a poor shelter useless at half its points, 40 down to 20; the hailstorm and cracked-pole mishaps aging a shelter before its time), the rest and comfort rules (no more than 16 hours per day in active adventuring, fatigue stops not counting as rest; camp chores in three hours at most; five hours of sleep every 24 hours to avoid the risk of ill effects that may not show up right away) and TABLE 37 EFFECTS OF LACK OF SLEEP (the five bands less than 5/4/3/2/1 hours average rest per day: Dexterity Checks at +1/+2/+3/+4/+5; Strength at +1/+2/+3/+4 from the second band; Wisdom at +1/+2/+3 from the third; Constitution at +1/+2 in the bottom two; to-hit -1/-1/-2/-3; Climbing Rating -10/-20/-30 percent; Movement Rate -25/-33/-50 percent; Weight Allowance -50 and -100 x Strength), printed pp. 63-64.
banner.provenance: Ground truth two-way on the prose, three-way on the contested grid cells, no physical-page reads: the user-run Termux tesseract text of printed pp. 63-64 (p63_full.txt, p64_full.txt) vs the pdf embedded text layer (pdftotext -layout, pdf pages 64-65, p63_64_pdfy.txt). The two readers AGREE on all prose numbers: the 2/4/6 pole minimums, the occupancy counts, the 1-turn helper saving, the 1/2/3-turn setup minimums, the one-turn-less takedown with the 5-round/1-turn/2-turn minimums, the 10-mph/5-mph wind leak step, the twice-threshold 25% damage chance, the 1/3-use and 1/2/4 life span point rates, the poor 40-to-20 collapse, the 16/3/5-hour rules, the two-day trigger, the one-night negation and the 12-to-6 movement example. For the TABLE 37 GRID the tesseract TSV geometry and full text carry every cell EXCEPT the LESS-THAN-2 DEXTERITY AND STRENGTH cells, which tesseract garbles into low-confidence noise: the pdf layer reads them as Dexterity Checks at +4 and Strength Checks at +3, and a VISION READ of the uploaded page image (pg-001-2.png) SECOND-CONFIRMS the full grid including those two contested cells - the R471 vision-on-png combo as the standing contested-cell settler. The grid is also internally consistent: each ability ladder steps exactly one per band, and the less-than-5 band carries the Dexterity entry alone.
banner.sentinel: All 40 Table 37 cells pinned (the five bands by eight effect columns); the shelter kit mechanics, the setup and takedown discipline, the wind and moisture semantics, the life span economy, the rest and sleep rules and the book's own worked wind and movement examples are audit examples.

consts.name: wrsAdequateMinPoles
consts.comment: the adequate shelter kit includes at least two poles: one for a backbone (ridgepole) and one for a cross-brace

consts.name: wrsGoodMinPoles
consts.comment: the good kit: at least four poles - a ridgepole, a cross-brace and two side poles for added strength and stability

consts.name: wrsSuperiorMinPoles
consts.comment: the superior kit: at least six poles, enough to actually make a simple but strong frame for the cover

consts.name: wrsSmallComfort
consts.comment: a small shelter comfortably holds one human-sized character (or two smaller ones) plus all their personal gear

consts.name: wrsMediumComfort
consts.comment: a medium shelter easily accommodates two human-sized characters, or the equivalent in smaller characters

consts.name: wrsLargeDesign
consts.comment: a large shelter is designed to hold four human-sized characters

consts.name: wrsLargeSleepMax
consts.comment: a large shelter can sleep five or six men if the group stores some of its gear outside

consts.name: wrsLargeCloseMax
consts.comment: a large shelter holds seven or eight men in close quarters, and no more than eight can sleep inside it

consts.name: wrsSetupHelperSaving
consts.comment: a second character assisting with the setup reduces the time by 1 turn

consts.name: wrsSetupMinSmallTurns
consts.comment: it takes at least 1 turn to set up a small shelter

consts.name: wrsSetupMinMediumTurns
consts.comment: a medium shelter takes at least 2 turns to set up

consts.name: wrsSetupMinLargeTurns
consts.comment: a large shelter takes at least 3 turns to set up

consts.name: wrsTakedownSavingTurns
consts.comment: taking down the shelter and re-packing it takes 1 turn less than it took to put up

consts.name: wrsTakedownMinSmallRounds
consts.comment: at least five rounds to dismantle and pack a small shelter

consts.name: wrsTakedownMinMediumTurns
consts.comment: at least 1 turn to dismantle and pack a medium shelter

consts.name: wrsTakedownMinLargeTurns
consts.comment: at least 2 turns to dismantle and pack a large shelter

consts.name: wrsWindStepMph
consts.comment: for every 10 mph of actual wind velocity greater than the indicated number

consts.name: wrsWindLeakMph
consts.comment: those inside the tent feel a wind of 5 mph for each 10 mph step above the rating

consts.name: wrsWindDamageThresholdMult
consts.comment: the wind damage chance applies if the velocity exceeds twice the indicated number

consts.name: wrsWindDamagePctPerStep
consts.comment: a 25% chance for each 10 mph of additional velocity, checked each hour, that the wind damages the shelter

consts.name: wrsWindExPoorRes
consts.comment: the book wind example: a poor shelter provides complete protection up to 20 mph

consts.name: wrsWindEx30Leak
consts.comment: the book example: at 30 mph those inside feel a breeze of 5 mph

consts.name: wrsWindEx40Leak
consts.comment: the book example: at 40 mph the breeze inside is 10 mph

consts.name: wrsWindEx50Leak
consts.comment: the book example: at 50 mph the breeze inside is 15 mph

consts.name: wrsWindEx60Leak
consts.comment: the book example: at 60 mph the breeze inside has reached a hefty 20 mph

consts.name: wrsWindEx50DamagePct
consts.comment: the book example: at 50 mph a 25% chance per hour of wind damage

consts.name: wrsWindEx60DamagePct
consts.comment: the book example: at 60 mph a 50% chance per hour of wind damage

consts.name: wrsLifespanSetupsPerPoint
consts.comment: 1 life span point deducted for each three times the shelter is put up

consts.name: wrsLifespanWindPoints
consts.comment: 1 point for each exposure to wind speeds above its wind resistance that does no actual damage

consts.name: wrsLifespanEqualPrecipPoints
consts.comment: 2 points for each exposure to precipitation equal in intensity to its moisture resistance value

consts.name: wrsLifespanGreaterPrecipPoints
consts.comment: 4 points for each exposure to precipitation greater in intensity than its moisture resistance value

consts.name: wrsPoorLifespanMax
consts.comment: a poor shelter starts with 40 life span points

consts.name: wrsPoorUselessAt
consts.comment: a poor shelter losing half its maximum points (from 40 to 20) is useless until repaired

consts.name: wrsMaxActiveHours
consts.comment: a character should spend no more than 16 hours per day in active adventuring pursuits

consts.name: wrsCampChoreHours
consts.comment: setting up a shelter, hunting and foraging, and cooking the nighttime meal should all be done in three hours at most

consts.name: wrsSleepHoursNeeded
consts.comment: a character needs five hours of sleep every 24 hours to avoid the risk of ill effects from lack of rest

consts.name: wrsTriggerDays
consts.comment: the lack-of-sleep effects do not set in until a character has gone two days without at least five hours of sleep during one of them

consts.name: wrsExMoveRate
consts.comment: the book movement example: a character with a normal movement rate of 12

consts.name: wrsExHalfDayMiles
consts.comment: the book movement example: operating with less than 1 hour of sleep he can travel only 6 miles per half-day on foot

consts.name: wrsSleepBands
consts.comment: the Table 37 average-rest bands: less than 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 hours

consts.name: wrsRowCount
consts.comment: the Table 37 row count

bools.name: wrsPoorKitLooseStitching
bools.comment: the poor shelter "single piece" covering is actually several pieces loosely stitched with rawhide or cord neither particularly strong nor durable: wind easily finds its way in through the seams, and the covering does not completely keep out rain or snow because of its loose construction

bools.name: wrsPoorKitBringYourOwn
bools.comment: the poor kit provides no special anchoring equipment and no rope: the edges must be anchored with rocks or other weights at hand or handmade stakes whittled from branches, the characters provide their own rope, and an unskilled character manufacturing a portable shelter ends up with this quality

bools.name: wrsAdequateKitTighter
bools.comment: the adequate covering is made of multiple sections just as a poor one, but the edges are more closely matched and the stitching tighter and stronger: it does not let in wind or precipitation as easily, and its wooden or metal stakes are driven through the edges into the ground

bools.name: wrsGoodKitShingled
bools.comment: the good covering pieces are not only stitched tightly together but overlapped like shingles so no seams are directly exposed on the outer surface, and the edges contain reinforced holes through which a stake can be driven or a rope strung to anchor without damaging the material

bools.name: wrsSuperiorKitStructure
bools.comment: the superior covering is extremely well waterproofed, made of as few separate pieces as possible with joined seams reinforced by another thickness of material: a true structure keeping out all but the strongest wind and heaviest precipitation, the next best thing to finding a miner's shack

bools.name: wrsSmallCloseQuarters
bools.comment: the small shelter can be used to shelter up to twice as many occupants in close quarters

bools.name: wrsMediumCloseQuarters
bools.comment: the medium shelter holds up to twice as many in close quarters

bools.name: wrsLargeCloseQuartersOnly8
bools.comment: no more than eight can sleep inside a large shelter without some of the occupants being literally on top of others

bools.name: wrsSetupAssumesRope
bools.comment: the poor and adequate setup times assume the characters have rope and, for a poor shelter, some objects with which to anchor the cover

bools.name: wrsRopeUseHalvesSetup
bools.comment: a character with proficiency in rope use sets up the shelter, with or without help, in half the time (rounded up) indicated by the die roll

bools.name: wrsTakedownNoHelperBonus
bools.comment: the takedown time is 1 turn less than the setup time regardless of how many characters assist

bools.name: wrsRopeUseHalvesTakedown
bools.comment: a character with proficiency in rope use can dismantle and properly pack a shelter in half the time it takes a nonproficient character

bools.name: wrsMoistureOneStepLighter
bools.comment: precipitation heavier than the moisture resistance value gets through the shelter and falls on the occupants as though they were in a storm one step lighter in intensity (a poor shelter douses its occupants in a moderate storm as if they were in the open during a light one)

bools.name: wrsSuperiorDownpourCaveat
bools.comment: a superior shelter protects those inside from even a downpour, as long as the wind is not too strong and the force of the storm does not separate the shelter from its moorings

bools.name: wrsWindLeakRule
bools.comment: the wind resistance number is the greatest wind velocity the shelter withstands without leaking, and the effective temperature inside changes with the leaked breeze

bools.name: wrsWindDamageUseless
bools.comment: a wind-damaged shelter is useless until it is repaired

bools.name: wrsLifespanAsHitPoints
bools.comment: life span may be thought of as the shelter's hit points: a new or freshly repaired shelter has the indicated number of life span points

bools.name: wrsCategoryDegradation
bools.comment: when a superior, good or adequate shelter loses enough points to bring it down to the maximum value of the next lower category, it is treated as a shelter of that category until it deteriorates completely or is repaired

bools.name: wrsPoorHalfUseless
bools.comment: repair costs and availability are in the province of the DM, but hauling a dilapidated poor shelter into town to be fixed would cost more effort and time than it is worth: cut up the cover and make it into sacks or saddle blankets

bools.name: wrsLifespanHazards
bools.comment: the life span does not account for mishaps that age a shelter early: a hailstorm may at the DM discretion punch holes or weaken the seams, a tent pole cracked flailing on a wild bear will not hold the cover in a stiff wind, but barring such occurrences most shelters serve well for an adventure or two or longer

bools.name: wrsActiveTimeCap
bools.comment: the 16-hour active time includes rest stops taken to avoid fatigue, which do not count as actual rest for these rules; the remainder of the day is set aside for making camp, eating and sleeping

bools.name: wrsSleepRiskHidden
bools.comment: an improperly rested character's ill effects may not show up right away, might not manifest themselves at all if he is lucky, or might come back to haunt him at a very inopportune time

bools.name: wrsTwoDayTrigger
bools.comment: a character can stay up all night and function normally throughout the next day, but if he does not get at least five hours of sleep on the following night then the effects begin at sunrise or when he awakens

bools.name: wrsDayByDayCalc
bools.comment: average rest per day is calculated on a day-by-day basis whenever a character goes two or more consecutive days without getting at least five hours of sleep during one of those days

bools.name: wrsOneNightNegation
bools.comment: as soon as he gets five hours of sleep in a single day, any and all effects are negated: the character is replenished by one good night's sleep even after several deprived days in a row

bools.name: wrsCheckModifierOnRoll
bools.comment: the table modifiers are applied to the die roll whenever an Ability Check or a Proficiency Check related to the indicated ability is called for

bools.name: wrsMoveReductionAfterAdjustments
bools.comment: the movement rate entries reduce the character's normal large-scale movement rate, taken after all other adjustments for terrain and encumbrance are accounted for

bools.name: wrsCombatMoveExempt
bools.comment: the movement penalty does not apply in combat situations or other feet-per-round movement: ambushed while travelling 6 miles per half-day, the character still moves at his full rate while the combat episode is resolved

TABLE 36, printed p. 62 - the second camping-arc round
and the second TABLE ROUND of the arc: the p. 61 seam tail
(a cave in the face of a mountain slope is a superior
shelter in all respects, assuming the opening faces away
from the wind; the DM judgment prevailing in any
circumstances not covered by the guidelines), the hauling
rules (a single mount or size M pack animal easily
transporting all the gear for many shelter types with
plenty of carrying capacity left over; in the absence of
an animal a single average-strength character hauling on
his back enough for himself and a small group at their
rest stops), the simplest form (a single wooden pole of
6-10 feet plus a fairly large expanse of heavy waterproofed
cloth or similarly pliable material; the DM may allow a
two- or three-piece pole apparatus held by lashings or
pegs, easier to transport), the pitch rules (the pole
anchored at 30 to 45 degrees, the covering draped over
it, the edges tied down with ropes and stakes, the
opening facing opposite the wind), the occupancy (one
human or a pair of smaller characters, and in a pinch
two men with no appreciable loss of protection or
comfort), the escalation (more elaborate shelters for
vicious weather or a decent-sized group huddling in one
tent) and the Table 36 grid (the four quality bands
poor/adequate/good/superior by small/medium/large:
GOOD LARGE 1d4+2 OUTLIER breaking the 1d3+ pattern of
its band, verified in all three readers; moisture light/
moderate/heavy/downpour; wind 20/30/40/50 pct; life span
